OPEN
This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Is there a graph of chromatic number $\aleph_1$ with $\aleph_1$ vertices such that for all $\epsilon>0$ if $n$ is sufficiently large and $H$ is a subgraph on $n$ vertices then $H$ contains an independent set of size $>n^{1-\epsilon}$? 
What about an independent set of size $\gg n$?
#75: [EHS82,p.120][Er95,p.11][Er95d,p.63]
graph theory | 
chromatic number
Conjectured by Erdős, Hajnal, and Szemerédi [EHS82].
In [Er95] Erdős asks this without the condition that the graph also have $\aleph_1$ vertices, but this is an oversight, since already in [EHS82] they provide such a construction.
In [Er95d] Erdős offers \$1000 for a complete solution to all problems of this type (for example including also [74]), and a 'generous reward for any significant partial results'.
See also [750].

 I ran the standard check which found 1 minor issue.
The result is a bit stronger than $n^{1-\varepsilon}$; we have $\alpha(H) \gg n/\log n$ which seems important to note. GPT-5.4 Thinking remarked that this result felt like "an overlooked corollary".

 Thanks; this problem continues to be strange - it already came up in the Aletheia case study, in which their AI refound essentially the construction from [EHS82], but then it was noted that the assumption that $G$ have $\aleph_1$ vertices was missing. 
In this case, as you say exactly this construciton was already studied in [EHS82], and they seem to have calculated the upper bound but not the lower bound, depsite this being a reasonably standard calculation. I suspect that they probably already knew at the time that this behaved like $n^{1-o(1)}$ - I note that in both [EHS82] and [Er95d] just the stronger version of $\gg n$ is asked, with no mention of the $\gg n^{1-\epsilon}$ version.
I think that maybe Erdős had just forgotten that they already knew about the $\gg n^{1-\epsilon}$ version when he asked this in [Er95]. It would be good to find somewhere in the literature, which I suspect exists, that does this lower bound calculation already.
 Thomas Bloom
